```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library("naboer")
library("tibble")
library("mgcv")
library("datasets")

have_gratia <- requireNamespace("gratia", quietly = TRUE)
if (have_gratia) {
  library("gratia")
  library("ggplot2")
}
```

naboer builds the `nei` argument that mgcv uses to select smoothness by
neighbourhood cross-validation (NCV) or its quadratic variant (QNCV).

## Fit a model with mgcv

How smooth a curve would you use to estimate the water level in the middle
of a five-year gap in the record? To mimic that prediction task, leave out
the year to be predicted and the two years on either side, then score the
prediction for the middle year.

R includes annual measurements of Lake Huron water levels from 1875 to 1972.
Use the calendar year as the model predictor and the start of each year
as the index for constructing folds. The recorded levels are in feet.
[Lake Huron data documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/datasets/html/LakeHuron.html).

```{r lake-data}
year <- as.integer(time(LakeHuron))
lake <- tibble(
  year = year,
  date = as.Date(sprintf("%d-01-01", year)),
  level = as.numeric(LakeHuron)
)
```

Create one fold per year with a window that reaches two calendar years
before and after the target. Near the ends of the record it includes only
the neighbours that are available.

```{r lake-folds}
lake_folds <- neighbourhoods(lake,
  index = date, temporal = temporal_window(time_span(2, "years", type = "calendar"))
)
```

Check the fold for 1925. The **assessment** is the year whose prediction is
scored. The **omission** includes the assessment year and its neighbours,
1923 to 1927. The remaining years make up the **analysis** data used for
fitting that fold.

```{r inspect-lake-fold}
lake_data <- fold_data(lake_folds)
target <- match(1925L, lake_data$year)
lake_data$year[assessment_indices(lake_folds, folds = target)[[1]]]
lake_data$year[omission_indices(lake_folds, folds = target)[[1]]]
```

The exported indices refer to rows of `fold_data()`. Pass those data to
`as_nei()` to check the alignment and use the same data to fit the model.
If you change the observations, rebuild the folds before fitting.

```{r lake-nei}
lake_nei <- as_nei(lake_folds, data = lake_data)
```

Fit water level as a smooth function of year. Supply `nei` and
`method = "NCV"` to `gam()` to choose smoothness using the five-year windows.

```{r lake-ncv}
lake_ncv <- gam(level ~ s(year, k = 20),
  data = lake_data, method = "NCV", nei = lake_nei, na.action = na.fail
)
```

Fit the same model with `nei` omitted. With `method = "NCV"`, mgcv
then leaves out only the year it scores. Both final fits use the full record,
with the smoothing parameter chosen by their respective criteria.

```{r lake-loo}
lake_loo <- gam(level ~ s(year, k = 20),
  data = lake_data, method = "NCV", na.action = na.fail
)
```

Use gratia to compare the effective degrees of freedom (EDF) of the two
smooths. The fit selected with the five-year window has lower EDF and follows
broader changes in water level.

```{r lake-edf, eval=have_gratia}
tibble(
  criterion = c("Leave-one-out", "Five-year window"),
  effective_degrees_of_freedom = c(edf(lake_loo)$.edf, edf(lake_ncv)$.edf)
)
```

Use `add_fitted()` to attach the fitted values to their years for plotting.

```{r lake-curve-data, eval=have_gratia}
lake_curves <- rbind(
  transform(add_fitted(lake_data, lake_loo, value = "fitted_level"),
    criterion = "Leave-one-out"
  ),
  transform(add_fitted(lake_data, lake_ncv, value = "fitted_level"),
    criterion = "Five-year window"
  )
)
```

Overlay the two fitted curves on the observed water levels.

```{r lake-curves, eval=have_gratia, fig.width=7, fig.height=4, dev.args=list(bg="white"), fig.alt="Observed annual water levels at Lake Huron and two fitted curves. The curve selected with the five-year window follows broader changes than the leave-one-out curve."}
ggplot(lake_data, aes(x = year)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = level), colour = "grey50", size = 1.2) +
  geom_line(
    data = lake_curves,
    aes(y = fitted_level, colour = criterion, linetype = criterion),
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Five-year window" = "#0072B2", "Leave-one-out" = "#D55E00"
  )) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Water level (feet)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Use `method = "QNCV"` for mgcv's quadratic approximation to the score.
For a Gaussian model with the identity link, as above, the loss is already
quadratic. [mgcv NCV documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/NCV.html).

You can also use naboer to choose smoothness for
[soil moisture over time](temporal.html#choose-smoothness-for-a-time-series),
[daily maximum temperature across weather stations](spatial.html#choose-smoothness-for-spatial-data)
and [carbon dioxide uptake by plants](ecological.html#predict-carbon-dioxide-uptake-for-a-new-plant).

## Inspect a fold

Create eight observations in time order. We will score rows 3 and 6 in separate
folds, leaving out one extra row on either side of each target.

```{r example-data}
x <- tibble(time = 1:8, y = c(1, 2, 2, 4, 3, 5, 7, 6))
```

Use `custom_folds()` to specify the two sets of row numbers for each fold.

```{r make-folds}
folds <- custom_folds(x, assessment = list(3L, 6L), omission = list(2:4, 5:7))
```

The fold table shows how many rows are in each set. The `n_buffer` column
counts the extra omissions. They appear as `buffer_size` in `summary()` and
as `omitted` in plots.

```{r inspect-folds}
as_tibble(folds)
```

Inspect the row numbers for the first fold. Row 3 is scored, rows 2 and 4 are
also left out, and rows 1 and 5 to 8 are used for fitting.

```{r inspect-membership}
assessment_indices(folds, folds = 1)
omission_indices(folds, folds = 1)
analysis_indices(folds, folds = 1)
```

## Choose a design for the prediction task

Start with where, when or for whom the predictions will be made. The table shows
common starting points. The [fold design schematics](fold-designs.html) show
which observations each design uses for fitting and scoring.

| Prediction task | Design to consider |
|---|---|
| New observations from already sampled units | Leave-one-out or random V-fold, if neighbours in training reflect how predictions will be made |
| Predictions with no nearby training observations | Leave out a neighbourhood around each target, or add a buffer around each held-out block |
| New locations in the sampled region | Hold out spatial blocks |
| New periods | Hold out temporal blocks |
| Future observations given data available at the time | Use forecast origins, a horizon and, if needed, a gap |
| New groups | Hold out entire groups or combinations of grouping levels |
| New environments | Hold out groups defined by environmental predictors |
| New taxa | Hold out clades, distance-based blocks or neighbourhoods on a phylogenetic tree |

Spatial and temporal blocks can also separate the environmental conditions of
the training and assessment data. Larger errors may then reflect the difficulty
of predicting under unfamiliar conditions. Choose a design that represents the
range of conditions you expect to predict in. For neighbourhood designs, choose
the radius using knowledge of the system or a separate analysis of dependence.
Check that the model can be fitted and can make the required predictions in each
fold, especially if assessment rows contain factor levels absent from training.

Use a key to identify repeated units or series. Use `.by` when the data contain
independent domains and automatically generated neighbourhoods should stay
within each domain. Custom fold membership and existing exclusions are kept as
supplied. A V-fold design can allocate whole blocks from several domains to the
same fold. When forecasting, observations from other domains, including later
observations, can remain available for fitting. Define domains according to
which information would actually be available when making the prediction.

## Read the exported indices

To see how larger omissions are represented, export the original two-fold
design.

```{r export-indices}
as_nei(folds)
```

The vector `a` lists the omitted row numbers for each fold in turn, and `ma`
marks where each fold ends in that vector. Here `ma` is `c(3, 6)`, so the first
fold uses positions 1 to 3 and the second uses positions 4 to 6. The pair
`d` and `md` works the same way for assessment. If a row is assessed in several
folds, each assessment contributes to the criterion without automatic
reweighting.

When you pass your model data to `as_nei(data = ...)`, the alignment check
compares the row identifiers in order if you set `id` when constructing the
folds. Otherwise it compares all columns, including their order, types and values.
Export for mgcv requires at least two folds. You can inspect a single fold
in naboer or use its row indices for a separate refit.

### Sample folds in bam

`bam()` supports NCV with `discrete = TRUE`. To choose smoothness with a
sample of folds, keep the full design and pass `sample` to `as_nei()`.
The [Mauna Loa example](performance.html#fitting-with-sampled-neighbourhoods)
fits a trend and seasonal cycle using this approach.

### Covariance and standard errors

Wood's dependence-adjusted covariance assumes one assessment fold per
observation, reciprocal neighbourhoods, and negligible residual correlation
outside each neighbourhood. Reciprocity means that whenever row `j` is in
row `i`'s neighbourhood, row `i` is also in row `j`'s. Asymmetric windows can
still define a cross-validation score.

On affected mgcv releases, `as_nei()` puts folds in data row order for
covariance calculations when each observation has exactly one fold assessing
it alone. It also translates any explicit sample numbers to that order. On
those releases, requesting raw jackknife covariance with `jackknife = TRUE`
requires this assessment layout.

In mgcv 1.9-5, the default dependence-adjusted covariance in `gam()` can count
a model offset twice.
Use `as_nei(folds, jackknife = FALSE)` if standard Bayesian covariance is
appropriate for your model. For discrete `bam()` in that release, check that
prediction standard errors are finite and that the covariance matrix has no
substantially negative eigenvalues. A sample of one fold can also trigger a
warning about taking a maximum over an empty set.

`bam()` applies NCV to a penalised linear approximation of the model. An exact
non-Gaussian refit uses the full loss function. The implementation in `bam()` is
designed for small neighbourhoods and can be expensive when folds omit large
blocks. [mgcv NCV documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/NCV.html),
[mgcv bam documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/mgcv/html/bam.html).

## Check the approximation for large omissions

For non-quadratic loss functions, NCV approximates what happens to the fitted
model when observations are left out. QNCV also uses a quadratic approximation
to the score, which keeps the criterion finite for supported models. The two
methods can differ in how closely they match an exact refit. Wood's accuracy
result as sample size increases assumes the neighbourhood size stays fixed.
Check accuracy separately for designs that omit large blocks or much of the
future record at each forecast origin.

The repository's benchmark compares both criteria with exact refits. It holds
the smoothing parameter and the basis for the smooth fixed to isolate the effect
of the approximation. [Approximation script](https://github.com/gavinsimpson/naboer/blob/main/benchmarks/approximation.R).

For 120 observations, seed 20261017 and a smoothing parameter of 0.2, relative
differences in the Gaussian scores were below `1e-12`. In the Poisson example,
the differences varied with the radius of the temporal window.

| Temporal radius | Maximum omitted fraction | NCV relative criterion error | QNCV relative criterion error |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 7 | 12.5% | 0.23% | 0.47% |
| 15 | 25.8% | 6.04% | 15.10% |
| 30 | 50.8% | 0.37% | 25.37% |
| 48 | 80.8% | 15.36% | 68.98% |

These results describe one simulated data set. The error can rise or fall as the
window gets wider, and an accurate total score can hide discrepancies in
individual predictions. The script also checks whether refits converge and
records the largest NCV prediction difference on the scale of the model's
linear predictor. For your own model, compare both scores and predictions
across representative folds and smoothing parameters. If the approximation is
unsuitable, use `as_rset()` to export the folds for explicit refitting.
